title: GitHub: Your Home Base for Building with AI
description: GitHub from absolute zero: version control without the jargon, git essentials for daily work, pull requests and collaboration, plus Actions, Pages, Codespaces, and workflows for AI-assisted builders. No prior experience needed.

lessons.title: Version Control: Save Points for Your Work
lessons.bodyMd:
## The problem every builder hits

You build something. It works. You feel great. Then you change one small thing, and everything breaks. You stare at the screen trying to remember what you changed. Was it that file? That line? An hour ago or three? This is not a beginner problem. Professionals with twenty years of experience hit this wall. The only difference is that professionals have a system that makes the wall disappear.

## Save points, but for everything

If you have ever played a video game with save points, you already understand version control. Before a hard boss fight, you save. If the fight goes badly, you reload. You never lose more than a few minutes of progress, and you can experiment freely because the save point is always there.

Version control gives your projects save points. Every time your work reaches a good state, you take a snapshot. If a later change breaks things, you can look at exactly what changed between snapshots, or roll back to the last good one. No guessing. No panic.

## The four superpowers

Version control gives you four abilities that change how you build:

**Snapshots.** Save the exact state of every file in your project with one command. Not a zip file on your desktop named final-v2-REALLY-final. A real, labeled snapshot stored properly.

**History.** Every snapshot comes with a note explaining what changed and why. Six months from now, you can read the story of how your project grew, decision by decision.

**Time travel.** Jump your entire project back to any snapshot. Broke something on Friday? Go back to Thursday's snapshot, see what is different, and fix it with facts instead of guesses.

**Comparison.** See exactly what changed between any two snapshots, line by line. This turns "something broke and I do not know what" into "these three lines changed, and one of them is the problem."

## Why this matters before you write code

Here is the part most tutorials skip: version control is not just for code. Writers use it for manuscripts. Designers use it for mockups. AI builders use it for prompts, configurations, datasets, and the code their AI assistants generate.

The moment you start building anything you care about, you want save points. Not after you are "good enough." Now. Beginners benefit the most, because beginners experiment the most, and experiments are exactly what save points are for.

## The one-sentence version

Version control is a system that takes labeled snapshots of your work so you can compare, undo, and understand every change you ever make. Git is the most popular version control tool, and GitHub is where most people store their git snapshots online. The rest of this guide makes both of them yours.

lessons.title: Git vs GitHub: The Tool and the Home
lessons.bodyMd:
## Two names, two jobs

Beginners mix up git and GitHub constantly, because the names are almost identical and they always appear together. They are two different things with two different jobs. Once you separate them, everything gets clearer.

## Git: the tool on your computer

Git is a free program that runs on your machine. It watches a folder, takes snapshots when you ask it to, and stores the full history right there on your computer. It works offline. It does not need an account. It does not need the internet. Linus Torvalds, the creator of Linux, built it in 2005 because he needed a better way to track changes to a massive project, and it has been the industry standard ever since.

Think of git as a camera. It takes the snapshots. It holds the photo album. Everything it does happens locally, in your hands.

## GitHub: the home on the internet

GitHub is a website (and company, now owned by Microsoft) that hosts git repositories online. A repository, or repo, is just a project folder that git is tracking. GitHub gives that repo a home on the internet where it is backed up, shareable, and visible to others.

Think of GitHub as the photo-sharing site. Your camera (git) takes the photos. The site (GitHub) stores them safely, lets you share albums, and lets friends add their own photos to shared albums.

## Side by side

| | Git | GitHub |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A program on your computer | A website and hosting service |
| Needs internet | No | Yes |
| Needs an account | No | Yes |
| Stores your history | Yes, locally | Yes, as a synced copy |
| Lets others collaborate | Not by itself | Yes, that is its superpower |
| Costs money | Never, it is free and open source | Free for the essentials, paid tiers for teams |

## Do you need both?

Technically, no. You can use git alone forever and never touch GitHub. Plenty of people track personal projects locally with git and never upload anything.

Practically, yes, you want both. GitHub is where your work gets backed up (your laptop can die, GitHub will not), where collaborators join in, where employers look at your code, and where deployment services like Vercel connect to ship your projects live. Git does the tracking. GitHub makes the tracking useful to the world.

## The vocabulary you now own

You now know the three words this whole guide is built on. **Git** is the snapshot tool. A **repository** is a tracked project. **GitHub** is the online home for repositories. Every lesson from here on is just detail on top of those three ideas.

lessons.title: Why Every AI Builder Needs GitHub
lessons.bodyMd:
## AI writes fast. You need a net.

AI coding assistants can generate in an afternoon what used to take a week. That speed is thrilling and dangerous. When code appears that fast, you cannot hold all of it in your head. You need a system that remembers every version of everything, because you will want to compare what the AI wrote on Monday with what it rewrote on Thursday, and understand why the Thursday version broke.

GitHub is that system. Every AI-assisted project should live in a git repository from the first prompt. The AI goes fast. Version control makes fast safe.

## Your work survives your laptop

Laptops get stolen, dropped, and drowned in coffee. Hard drives fail, usually the week before something important. A project that exists only on your machine is one accident away from not existing at all.

Push your work to GitHub and it lives in two places: your computer and GitHub's servers. Delete the local copy, lose the laptop, switch machines, and your project is one download away. This is the cheapest insurance in all of building.

## Push to deploy: the magic pipeline

Here is where it gets fun. Services like Vercel, Netlify, and Railway connect directly to your GitHub repositories. You push new code to GitHub, and seconds later your live website updates automatically. No manual uploading. No FTP. No "wait, did I upload the right file."

This pipeline, called continuous deployment, is how modern builders ship. You will set up your first one in Chapter 5, and once you feel it, you will never go back to manual uploads.

## Proof of work

"Show me what you have built" is the most common request in tech hiring, freelancing, and partnerships. A GitHub profile full of real projects answers that question before it is asked. Employers browse profiles the way other industries browse portfolios. A green contribution graph and a few well-documented projects say more than any resume bullet.

## Version everything, not just code

AI builders have more than code to track. Your best prompts deserve version control. Your AI tool configurations, your automation workflows, your datasets, your project notes: all of it benefits from snapshots and history. When a prompt that worked great in March stops working in June, you want to see exactly what changed.

## Collaboration with humans and AIs

Modern AI coding tools like Claude Code and Cursor are designed to work inside git repositories. They read your project structure, respect your branches, and their changes become commits you can review. Git is the shared language between you, your collaborators, and your AI assistants. Learn it once, and every tool you pick up later speaks it too.

lessons.title: The Social Coding Model
lessons.bodyMd:
## Code, out in the open

GitHub added something radical to version control: a social layer. Every repository can be public, which means anyone on earth can read your code, learn from it, and suggest improvements. This turned programming from a solitary activity into a shared global library.

## The core interactions

**Repository.** A project. It holds files, history, and a built-in website (the README) explaining what the project is.

**Star.** A bookmark that says "I like this." Starring is how the community votes. Popular projects collect thousands of stars, which signals quality to newcomers.

**Fork.** Your own copy of someone else's repository. Forking is how open source collaboration starts: you copy a project, improve it, and propose your improvements back.

**Follow.** Like social media, but the feed is code. Follow builders you admire and watch what they ship.

**Contributions.** Every commit, issue, and pull request you make is recorded on your profile as a contribution, visualized as the famous green squares. It is a public record of your building habit.

## Open source: the free university

Millions of repositories are open source: free for anyone to read, use, and improve. This is the single greatest learning resource in programming. Stuck on a problem? Someone has solved it in public, and you can read their exact solution. Want to see how professionals structure a project? Browse theirs.

Open source runs on licenses, simple legal documents that say what others may do with the code. The MIT License, the most common one, basically says "do whatever you want, just keep this notice." You will pick one for your own projects in Chapter 2.

## Reading code is a superpower

Beginners think learning means writing. Experienced builders know that reading is half the skill. Reading well-written open source code teaches you patterns, conventions, and tricks no tutorial covers. GitHub makes the world's best codebases readable in your browser with syntax highlighting and click-to-follow definitions. Use it like a library.

## Your place in it

You do not need permission to join. Create an account, publish something you built, star projects you admire, and you are part of the largest collaboration in human history. In Chapter 4, you will make your first contribution to someone else's project. For now, just know the door is open.

## Your first week on GitHub

Do not just read about the social model. Use it this week. Star five projects you actually use or admire: your editor, a library you like, a tutorial repo that helped you. Follow three builders whose work interests you: your feed will start showing real projects instead of emptiness. Pick one popular repository and read its README end to end, then click the Issues tab and read two open issues. You will learn more about how software gets built in that hour than in a week of tutorials.

## Discussions: the community living room

Many projects also have a **Discussions** tab: a forum for questions, ideas, and show-and-tell that do not fit the bug-or-feature mold of Issues. Stuck on how to use a library? Ask in Discussions before opening an issue. Built something cool with a tool? Share it there. Discussions are where the community hangs out, and regulars notice helpful newcomers.

lessons.title: Creating Your Account
lessons.bodyMd:
## The two-minute signup

Go to github.com and click Sign up. You will pick a username, enter your email, and create a password. That is the whole mechanical process. But a few choices you make here follow you for years, so let us make them well.

## Choosing a username

Your username appears in every repository URL you own (github.com/yourname/project) and on every commit you make. Pick something professional and lasting. Your name, or a variation of it, is the safest choice: patdiamitani beats xX_codeSlayer_Xx for every purpose that matters. Avoid numbers you will outgrow and jokes you will stop finding funny. You can change it later, but links to your old name break, so choose like it is permanent.

## The email decision

Use an email you will keep. GitHub lets you add multiple emails and keep your real address private (it can show a faceless noreply address on your commits instead). Turn on "Keep my email addresses private" in settings unless you have a reason not to. Your commit history is public; your inbox does not have to be.

## Turn on two-factor authentication now

Do this today, not someday. Go to Settings, then Password and authentication, and enable two-factor authentication with an authenticator app on your phone. Your GitHub account will eventually hold the keys to your projects, your deployments, and your professional reputation. A password alone is not enough. This takes three minutes and prevents the most common account disasters.

## Verify and explore

Confirm your email via the link GitHub sends. Then take the tour: the homepage shows a feed of activity from people you follow, the top bar has search (which searches all of GitHub's public code, a staggering resource), and the plus menu is where new repositories are born. You are set up. Next lesson: making the profile behind that username worth visiting.

## What the free plan includes

The free tier is genuinely generous: unlimited public and private repositories, a monthly allowance of Actions automation minutes, GitHub Pages hosting, and community support. You can learn, build a portfolio, host sites, and collaborate without paying anything. Paid plans add more automation minutes, advanced security features, and team management tools. You will know when you need them; until then, free covers everything in this guide.

## Make exploring a habit

Two pages deserve bookmarks. The **Explore** page (github.com/explore) surfaces trending repositories and topics: a daily window into what the builder community is excited about. And **search** is a superpower: you can search all public code on earth. Looking for an example of a login form in React? Search it, filter by language, and read real implementations. Get comfortable searching GitHub the way you search the web; it is one of the highest-leverage habits in this guide.

lessons.title: A Profile That Gets You Hired
lessons.bodyMd:
## Your profile is a landing page

When someone clicks your username, they see your profile: your avatar, bio, and an overview of your work. Recruiters, clients, and collaborators judge it in seconds. The good news: a strong profile takes an afternoon to build and pays off for years.

## The pieces that matter

**Avatar.** Use a clear photo of you, or a clean logo if you prefer. The default gray silhouette signals "I signed up and vanished." A real image signals a real person.

**Bio.** One or two lines: who you are and what you build. "AI builder shipping automation tools. Learning in public." beats a blank bio every time. Add your location and a link to your site or portfolio.

**Profile README.** This is the secret weapon. Create a repository named exactly like your username (github.com/yourname/yourname), add a README, and its contents appear at the top of your profile. Use it for a short intro, what you are working on, your skills, and how to reach you. Keep it skimmable: headers, a few bullet points, maybe stats or badges. This is the first thing visitors read.

**Pinned repositories.** You can pin up to six repositories to your profile. Pin your best work: projects with good READMEs, live demos, and real functionality. A pinned repo with a clear description and a screenshot beats ten unpinned repos with names like test-final-2.

**Contribution graph.** Those green squares show your activity over the past year. Do not obsess over them, and never fake them, but know that consistent activity reads as reliability. Building in public, a little at a time, fills the graph naturally.

## The honesty rule

Everything on your profile should be work you actually did and can explain. A hiring manager will click into your pinned repos and ask about them. Two genuine projects you understand deeply beat ten tutorial copies you cannot explain. Curate for depth, not volume.

## Your afternoon checklist

Upload a photo. Write a two-line bio. Create your profile README repository. Pin your best two or three projects (or come back and pin them once Chapter 3 gets you building). Link your website. Done. Your profile now works for you while you sleep.

## What hiring managers actually click

Curious what happens after someone lands on your profile? They click your pinned repos first, then skim the README, then glance at recent commit activity. That order tells you exactly what to optimize: pinned repos with READMEs a stranger can understand in thirty seconds, and a commit history that shows steady, real work. Issues and pull requests count as contributions too, so helping on other people's projects fills your graph with meaningful activity, not just solo commits.

## Keep it alive

A profile is not a monument; it is a garden. Update your profile README when your focus changes. Re-pin repos as your best work evolves: the tutorial project that impressed you in month one should give way to original work by month six. Archive or unpin experiments that no longer represent you. Fifteen minutes of pruning every few months keeps the profile honest and sharp.

lessons.title: Your First Repository
lessons.bodyMd:
## Birth of a repo

Click the plus menu in the top bar, then New repository. This page looks simple, but every field matters. Let us walk through it.

## Name and description

**Repository name:** short, lowercase, hyphens instead of spaces. my-first-website, not "My First Website!!". This name becomes part of the URL, so make it clean.

**Description:** one sentence saying what the project is. "A personal site built while learning HTML" is perfect. Descriptions show up in search results and on your profile, so write them like a human explaining the project to a friend.

## Public or private

**Public** means anyone can see it. **Private** means only you (and people you invite) can see it. For learning projects, public is usually better: it builds your profile, lets others help, and future you will enjoy the history. Keep things private when they contain secrets (API keys, passwords, client data) or work you are not ready to share. You can flip a repo from private to public later with two clicks.

## The three checkboxes

**Add a README file.** Check this. The README is the front page of your project: what it is, how to use it, how to run it. Every repo deserves one. You will write a good one in spirit throughout this guide; for now, the default template is fine.

**Add .gitignore.** A .gitignore file tells git which files to never track: passwords, API keys, temporary files, giant datasets. Pick the template matching your project type (Node, Python, and others) and you are protected from the most common beginner disaster: accidentally publishing secrets.

**Choose a license.** This tells others what they may do with your code. The MIT License is the friendly default: anyone can use your code for anything, including commercial projects, as long as they credit you. If you are unsure, choose MIT. No license actually means "all rights reserved," which confuses potential users, so picking one is kinder than picking none.

## Click Create, and look around

You now own a repository. The main page shows your files (just the README for now), the commit history ("Initial commit"), and buttons you will soon know by heart: Code (download options), Add file, and the pencil icon to edit. The About section on the right shows your description. Congratulations: you have published on GitHub. Next, let us put files in it without touching the terminal.

## Touring your new repo

Scroll down: your README renders as a formatted page below the file list. That is what visitors see first, which is why READMEs matter so much. On the right, the About section has a gear icon: click it to add **topics**, short tags like `javascript`, `ai`, or `portfolio` that make your repo discoverable in search. Add the website field if the project has a live demo. These small touches take a minute and make your work findable.

lessons.title: Uploading Files in the Browser
lessons.bodyMd:
## No terminal required

Everything in this lesson happens in your browser. GitHub's web interface handles the fundamentals: adding files, editing them, and saving versions. You can do real version control today and learn the terminal commands in Chapter 3 when you are ready.

## Uploading files

Open your repository and click **Add file**, then **Upload files**. Drag files from your computer into the browser, or click to browse. You can upload an entire small project this way: HTML files, images, documents, whatever the project needs.

Before you click the green button, look at the **Commit changes** box. GitHub asks for a short message describing what you did ("Add homepage and styles"). This message becomes part of the project's permanent history. Write it like a note to your future self, because that is exactly what it is. Then click **Commit changes**. Your files are now versioned.

## Editing in the browser

Click any file, then the pencil icon. You are now editing the file directly on GitHub. Change some text, scroll down, write a commit message ("Fix typo in headline"), and commit. You just made and saved a new version of your project without installing anything.

This is perfect for quick fixes: typos, small text changes, updating a README. Professionals do this daily.

## Creating files from scratch

**Add file**, then **Create new file**. Name it (index.html, notes.md, anything), type or paste content, commit. You can build an entire small website this way: create index.html, create style.css, commit each one, and you have a versioned project.

## What you just learned, translated

Every commit you made in the browser is a real git commit: a snapshot with your name, a timestamp, and your message, stored in the project's history. Click the commit history link (the clock icon) to see the timeline of everything you have done. The terminal commands in Chapter 3 do exactly what these buttons do; the buttons just hide the mechanics. You already understand the concepts. The terminal is just a faster way to do the same things.

## Renaming and deleting, also in the browser

Click any file and you will see the pencil (edit) and trash (delete) icons. Renaming works through the edit view: change the filename at the top, and GitHub records it as a rename. Deleting asks for a commit message like everything else ("Remove outdated draft"). Every one of these actions is a real commit in your history, with your name on it. The browser is a complete, if slower, version control client.

## Reading the history

Click the commit count link (it says something like "5 commits") to open the timeline. Each entry shows the message, the author, and the time. Click any commit to see exactly what changed in it: green additions, red deletions. This view is your project's diary. When something breaks next month, this is where you will come to find out what changed and when.

lessons.title: Installing Git and Setting It Up
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why leave the browser

The web interface is lovely for small changes, but real projects live on your computer, where your editor, your AI tools, and your terminal are. To work locally and sync with GitHub, you need git itself installed. This lesson gets you set up in ten minutes.

## Installing

Go to **git-scm.com** and download the installer for your system. On Mac, you can also install it with Homebrew (`brew install git`). On Windows, the installer adds Git Bash, a terminal that understands git commands. On most Linux systems, `sudo apt install git` does it.

Verify the install by opening your terminal and running:

```bash
git --version
```

If it prints a version number like `git version 2.45.0`, you are in business.

## Introducing yourself to git

Git stamps every snapshot with an author name and email. Tell it who you are once, and it remembers forever:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
```

Use the same email as your GitHub account. This is what connects your local commits to your GitHub profile, which is what fills in those green contribution squares. The `--global` flag means "apply to everything I do on this machine," so you only do this once.

## One more setting

Make sure new repositories use `main` as the default branch name (this matches GitHub's default and avoids confusion later):

```bash
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

## The everyday loop

Nearly all git usage boils down to three commands you will run dozens of times a day:

```bash
git add .                    # stage your changes (pick what goes in the snapshot)
git commit -m "Your message" # take the snapshot with a descriptive note
git push                     # upload your snapshots to GitHub
```

Add, commit, push. That rhythm is 90 percent of git. The next lesson puts it into motion with a real repository.

## A note on editors

Git sometimes opens a text editor (for longer commit messages, for example). If you find yourself stuck in a strange screen, you are probably in Vim: press `i` to type, `Esc` to stop typing, then type `:wq` and press Enter to save and quit. Or avoid the situation entirely by always using `git commit -m "message"` with the `-m` flag, which skips the editor.

## Check your work

Verify everything took effect:

```bash
git config --list
```

You should see your name, email, and default branch in the output. If something looks wrong, just run the `git config` command again with the right value; settings overwrite cleanly. Getting this right now means every commit you make from today on is properly attributed to you on GitHub.

lessons.title: Clone, Push, Pull: The Daily Rhythm
lessons.bodyMd:
## Cloning: downloading a repo

You made a repository on GitHub in Chapter 2. Now let us get it onto your computer. On the repo page, click the green **Code** button and copy the HTTPS URL. In your terminal, navigate where you want the project to live, and run:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourname/your-repo.git
```

Git downloads the entire project: every file, plus the complete history of every snapshot ever taken. Move into it:

```bash
cd your-repo
```

You now have a local copy wired to GitHub. The word "clone" is literal: a full copy, history and all.

## The working loop

Here is the rhythm of a normal work session:

**1. Check where you stand.** Before doing anything, run:

```bash
git status
```

This tells you which files changed, which are staged, and whether your local copy is behind GitHub's. Run it constantly. It is the command that answers "what is going on right now."

**2. Make your changes.** Edit files in your editor, or let your AI assistant generate code. Work normally. Git watches quietly.

**3. Stage and snapshot.**

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add contact page layout"
```

`git add .` stages everything that changed (the dot means "this folder"). The commit takes the snapshot with your message.

**4. Upload.**

```bash
git push
```

Your snapshots travel to GitHub. Refresh the repo page and your changes are there, with your commit message in the history.

## Pulling: staying in sync

If you edited files on GitHub's website, or a collaborator pushed changes, your local copy is behind. Catch up with:

```bash
git pull
```

This downloads new snapshots and merges them into your files. Make pulling the first thing you do when you sit down to work: `git pull`, then start. It prevents the most common collaboration headaches.

## The full session, end to end

```bash
cd your-repo
git pull                  # start fresh
# ... do your work ...
git status                # see what changed
git add .                 # stage it
git commit -m "Describe the change"  # snapshot it
git push                  # upload it
```

Five commands. That is a complete professional workflow. Everything else in git is optimization on top of this loop.

## Signing in from the terminal

The first time you push, GitHub needs to verify it is you. The smoothest path is the GitHub CLI: install `gh`, run `gh auth login`, and follow the prompts to authenticate in your browser. Alternatively, git will prompt for credentials through your system's credential manager. Passwords no longer work directly at the command line; you will use either the CLI or a personal access token. The `gh auth login` route is the friendliest, and it takes two minutes.

lessons.title: Commits and Messages That Make Sense
lessons.bodyMd:
## What a commit really is

A commit is two things bundled together: a snapshot of your project at one moment, and a message explaining what changed and why. The snapshot is for the computer. The message is for humans: your future self, your teammates, anyone who reads the history wondering "why does this work this way."

## The staging area: the shopping cart

Between your files and the snapshot sits the **staging area**. `git add` puts files into it; `git commit` snapshots whatever is staged. Think of it like a shopping cart: you toss items in (`git add`), review the cart (`git status`), then check out (`git commit`).

Why the extra step? Because it lets you split your work into logical chunks. Changed three files but only two belong together? Stage those two, commit, then stage the third separately. Each commit tells one clean story.

See exactly what you are about to commit with:

```bash
git diff --staged
```

This shows the staged changes line by line. Review it before every commit. It catches mistakes: the debug line you forgot, the password you almost published.

## Messages that help vs. messages that haunt

Your commit message is a note to the future. Compare:

Bad:

- "fix"
- "stuff"
- "asdf"
- "final final v3"

Good:

- "Fix login crash when password field is empty"
- "Add dark mode toggle to settings page"
- "Update README with setup instructions"

The formula: start with a verb, say what changed, and add why if it is not obvious. Keep the first line under 72 characters. Your future self, debugging at midnight, will thank your past self for "Fix off-by-one error in pagination" instead of "bugfix."

## Commit small, commit often

A commit should be one logical change: one bug fix, one feature, one cleanup. Small commits are easier to review, easier to undo, and easier to understand. If you catch yourself writing "and" in a commit message ("Add login and fix header and update docs"), that is three commits wearing a trench coat. Split them.

A practical rule: commit every time you complete a thought. Finished the header layout? Commit. Fixed the typo? Commit. Got the API call working? Commit. You can always combine related commits later; you cannot recover granularity you never saved.

## Reading your history

```bash
git log --oneline
```

This prints your commit history as a clean list: short ID plus message, newest first. It is the story of your project. When something breaks, this list is where the investigation starts: which commit introduced the problem? The answer is usually one `git log` away.

lessons.title: Branches: Safe Sandboxes for Experiments
lessons.bodyMd:
## The parallel universe

A **branch** is a parallel copy of your project where you can experiment without touching the stable version. Your main line of work lives on the `main` branch. When you want to try something, you create a branch, do the risky work there, and only merge it back when it works.

The analogy: `main` is the published book. A branch is a photocopy you scribble on. If the scribbles are good, they go into the next edition. If they are terrible, you recycle the photocopy and the book never knew.

## Creating and switching

```bash
git switch -c add-dark-mode
```

This creates a branch called `add-dark-mode` and switches to it, in one command. (Older tutorials use `git checkout -b add-dark-mode`; same result, newer command is clearer.) Your files look identical, because a branch starts as a copy of where you were.

Now work normally: edit, `git add`, `git commit`. Your commits land on the new branch. `main` sits untouched, safe.

See all your branches anytime:

```bash
git branch
```

The one with the star is where you are.

## Merging: bringing it home

When the experiment works, bring it back:

```bash
git switch main
git merge add-dark-mode
```

Git combines the branch's changes into `main`. If nobody else touched the same lines, this just works: a clean merge, no drama. Then push:

```bash
git push
```

And clean up the finished branch:

```bash
git branch -d add-dark-mode
```

Branches are cheap and disposable. Create them freely, delete them when done. Professional developers sometimes create and delete dozens per week.

## Your first merge conflict (do not panic)

A **merge conflict** happens when two branches change the same lines of the same file. Git cannot decide which version wins, so it asks you. This is not an error. It is git being careful.

Open the conflicted file and you will see markers:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
Your version of the line
=======
The other branch's version of the line
>>>>>>> add-dark-mode
```

Everything between `<<<<<<<` and `=======` is your current branch's version. Everything between `=======` and `>>>>>>>` is the incoming version. Your job: edit the file to the correct final version (keep one, keep both, or write something new), then **delete the marker lines**. Save, then:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Resolve merge conflict in styles.css"
```

Done. The conflict is resolved and recorded like any other change.

## The mindset

Conflicts feel scary the first time and boring the tenth time. They mean two people (or you, twice) cared about the same code. Read both versions, pick the right outcome, remove the markers, commit. There is no way to break anything permanently: every version involved is still in your history.

lessons.title: Pull Requests, Step by Step
lessons.bodyMd:
## What a pull request is

A **pull request** (PR) is a proposal: "I changed some things on my branch. Please review them and pull them into the main branch." It is the heart of collaboration on GitHub. Instead of pushing directly to `main` and hoping for the best, you open a PR, humans (or robots) review it, and only then does it merge.

Even solo builders should use PRs. A PR is a pause button: a moment to re-read your own changes with fresh eyes before they become permanent. Many professionals require PRs for every change, including their own.

## The setup

PRs need a branch. Push your branch to GitHub:

```bash
git push -u origin add-dark-mode
```

(The `-u` links your local branch to the GitHub copy, so future pushes need just `git push`.)

## Opening the PR

Visit your repository on GitHub. A yellow banner appears: the branch "had recent pushes." Click **Compare & pull request**.

You will see a form with two critical fields:

**Title.** Short and descriptive: "Add dark mode toggle to settings." Not "updates" or "my changes."

**Description.** Explain three things: what changed, why it changed, and how to test it. A good description:

```
Adds a dark mode toggle to the settings page.

Users requested this in issue #42. The toggle saves
the preference in localStorage so it persists.

To test: open Settings, flip the toggle, reload the page.
```

Click **Create pull request**. Your proposal is now ready for review.

## What happens inside a PR

A PR page has three tabs you will live in:

**Conversation.** The discussion. Reviewers leave comments here, ask questions, request changes. You reply and push new commits to the same branch; the PR updates automatically.

**Commits.** Every snapshot on your branch, in order. Reviewers can see the story of how you built the change.

**Files changed.** The actual diff: every line added (green) and removed (red). This is where careful review happens.

## The lifecycle

A typical PR goes: opened, reviewed, discussed, updated with new commits, approved, merged. When it merges, your branch's changes join `main`, and you delete the branch. The PR remains as a permanent record: who proposed what, who reviewed it, what was discussed. It is documentation that writes itself.

## Your first PR today

You can do this right now: create a branch, change one line in your README, push, and open a PR against your own repo. Then merge it yourself. The mechanics take five minutes. The habit will serve every project you ever touch.

lessons.title: Code Review Without the Fear
lessons.bodyMd:
## Review is a conversation, not a trial

Code review feels personal the first time someone critiques your work. It is not. The code is under review; you are not. Every professional, from junior to principal, gets their code reviewed. The goal is shared: catch bugs, share knowledge, keep quality high. Teams that review well ship better software and learn faster.

## Giving good feedback

When you review someone's PR:

**Ask questions before declaring.** "What happens here if the list is empty?" beats "This is wrong." Questions invite explanation; declarations invite defensiveness.

**Be specific and point at lines.** Comment on the exact line, suggest the fix if you know it. "Consider using a Set here for faster lookups" helps. "This could be better" does not.

**Distinguish must from maybe.** "Blocking: this will crash when offline" versus "Nit: consider renaming to `isVisible`." Not every comment needs to block the merge.

**Praise what is good.** "Clean approach to the error handling" takes five seconds and makes the whole process human. Review is not a bug hunt; it is a collaboration.

## Receiving feedback gracefully

**Do not reply instantly.** Read comments, let them sit, then respond. The sting fades; the insight remains.

**Assume good intent.** Text strips tone. "Why did you do it this way?" is usually curiosity, not attack.

**Push back when you are right.** Reviewers are wrong sometimes. "I tried that approach; it broke the mobile layout because..." is a perfectly good response. Discussion improves the outcome.

**Say thanks.** Someone spent their time making your code better. Acknowledge it.

## The robots help too

**Automated checks** run on every PR: tests, linting, build verification. Green checks mean the machines are happy. Red checks mean something concrete failed; click through to see exactly what. Fix, push, watch them re-run.

**Copilot code review** can review PRs automatically, leaving line-by-line comments and an approval assessment signaling whether it considers the PR ready. Treat it like a diligent junior reviewer: useful for catching the obvious, not a replacement for human judgment on design and intent.

## Approving and merging

When review is done, an approved PR shows a green **Merge pull request** button. Click it, confirm, and your branch joins `main`. Delete the branch (GitHub offers a button). The PR closes, the history records everything, and the project moves forward. That loop, proposal to review to merge, is the heartbeat of professional software development.

## Review your own PRs first

Before requesting reviewers, review your own pull request: open the Files changed tab and read the entire diff top to bottom, as if a stranger wrote it. You will catch debug lines you forgot, typos in comments, and changes you did not mean to include. Run the code one more time from the branch. This five-minute self-review catches half of all review comments before anyone else spends time on them, and it is the fastest way to earn a reputation for clean PRs.

lessons.title: Issues, Boards, and Contributing to Open Source
lessons.bodyMd:
## Issues: the project's memory

An **Issue** is GitHub's built-in tracker for anything a project needs: bug reports, feature requests, questions, to-do items. Each issue gets a number (#42), a title, a discussion thread, and labels like `bug`, `enhancement`, or `good first issue`.

Before building anything new, check the issues. Someone may have reported your bug already, or requested your feature. Issues prevent duplicated work and give every task a home. When you reference an issue in a commit message or PR ("Fixes #42"), GitHub links them automatically, and merging the PR can close the issue. The project's history tells its own story.

## Project boards: the kanban view

For planning, GitHub offers **Projects**: kanban boards where issues and PRs become cards in columns like To Do, In Progress, Done. Drag a card across the board as work progresses. It is simple, visual, and lives next to the code instead of in a separate tool. Solo builders use boards to organize their own roadmap; teams use them to coordinate.

## Forking: your copy of the world

A **fork** is your personal copy of someone else's repository, living in your account. Forking does not affect the original. It gives you a sandbox where you have full permission to experiment with code you do not own.

## Your first open source contribution

Here is the complete flow, the same one used by millions of contributors:

**1. Find a project and a task.** Look for the `good first issue` label: maintainers tag beginner-friendly tasks with it. Read the issue, read the project's CONTRIBUTING file if it has one (it explains the project's rules).

**2. Fork and clone.** Click **Fork** on the project page, then clone *your fork*:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/yourname/the-project.git
```

**3. Branch and build.** Create a branch, make your change, commit it, push to your fork.

**4. Open the PR.** On *your fork's* page, click **Contribute**, then **Open pull request**. This proposes your change to the original project. Write a clear description referencing the issue ("Fixes #123").

**5. Respond to review.** Maintainers may request changes. Push new commits to your branch; the PR updates. When approved, they merge, and your code ships in a project used by strangers. There is no feeling quite like it.

## Etiquette that gets you welcomed back

Start small: typo fixes and documentation improvements are genuinely valuable first contributions. Read the contributing guide before coding. One issue per PR. Be patient: maintainers are volunteers, and review takes time. Say thanks when your PR merges. The open source world remembers kindness, and your merged PRs become permanent public proof of your skills.

lessons.title: GitHub Actions: Your Robot Assistant
lessons.bodyMd:
## What Actions does, in plain English

**GitHub Actions** is automation built into GitHub: "when this happens in my repository, run these steps on a computer." Push to `main`? Run the tests. Open a pull request? Check the code style. Publish a release? Deploy the website.

Think of it as a robot assistant that watches your repo around the clock and does the boring verification work instantly, every time, without being asked.

## Why builders love it

Before Actions, teams ran tests manually ("did anyone run the test suite?"), deployed by hand (error-prone), and discovered broken code days late. Actions moves all of that into the repository itself: the automation lives in files, versioned like everything else, visible to everyone. A new contributor gets the same checks you do, automatically.

## Your first workflow

Workflows are defined in YAML files inside `.github/workflows/`. Here is a complete, real example that runs tests on every push and pull request:

```yaml
name: Run tests

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test
```

Read it like English: "When code is pushed to main or a PR is opened, grab a fresh Ubuntu computer, check out my code, install Node 20, install dependencies, run the tests." Save this as `.github/workflows/test.yml`, commit, push, and click the **Actions** tab. You will watch your robot run.

## The anatomy, without fear

Every workflow has three parts: the **trigger** (`on:`: what starts it), **jobs** (groups of steps, which can run in parallel), and **steps** (individual commands or reusable actions from the marketplace). The marketplace holds thousands of pre-built steps: deploying to Vercel, publishing packages, sending notifications. You compose; you rarely build from scratch.

## Costs and limits

Public repositories get generous free usage. Private repos get a monthly allowance of free minutes on the free plan, which is plenty for learning and small projects. Minutes count while your steps run on GitHub's computers. Keep workflows lean, cache dependencies, and you will rarely think about billing.

## Start with one

Do not automate everything on day one. Pick the single most valuable check: run your tests on every PR. Add it, watch it catch its first real bug, and feel the shift. That is the moment automation stops being abstract and becomes something you trust.

## Watching it work

After you push, open the **Actions** tab in your repo. Each run appears as an entry: yellow while running, green when it passes, red when it fails. Click a run to see every step expand with its logs, line by line. When something fails, the logs tell you exactly which command broke and why. There is also a **Re-run** button for flaky failures. Reading these logs is a skill in itself, and it transfers directly to debugging any automated system.

lessons.title: Free Hosting with Pages and Coding Anywhere with Codespaces
lessons.bodyMd:
## GitHub Pages: your free web host

**GitHub Pages** turns a repository into a live website, free. It is perfect for portfolios, project documentation, landing pages, and anything static (HTML, CSS, JavaScript with no server).

Setup takes a minute: go to your repo's **Settings**, then **Pages**. Under "Build and deployment," choose **Deploy from a branch**, select `main` and the `/ (root)` folder, and save. GitHub builds your site and gives you a URL like `yourname.github.io/my-site`. Push an update to `main`, and the site rebuilds automatically.

## What to host there

**Your portfolio.** A personal site with your projects, each linking back to its repo. Employers click through from your profile to your site to your code: a complete story.

**Project docs.** Every serious project deserves documentation beyond the README. Pages hosts it beautifully, versioned alongside the code.

**Demos and landing pages.** Built a tool with an AI assistant? Put a live demo on Pages and share the link. "Try it here" beats screenshots.

**Custom domains.** Pages supports your own domain with free HTTPS. Buy `yourname.com`, point it at GitHub, and your free site looks fully professional. The settings page walks you through the DNS records.

## Codespaces: a dev environment in your browser

**GitHub Codespaces** is a complete development environment (VS Code, terminal, your repo) running in the cloud and accessible from your browser. Click the green **Code** button on any repo, switch to the **Codespaces** tab, and launch one. Seconds later you are coding with zero local setup.

This shines when: you are on a Chromebook or borrowed machine, you want to try a repo without installing its toolchain, or you are reviewing a PR and want to run the code. The environment can be defined by a `devcontainer.json` file in the repo, so every contributor gets the identical setup. No more "works on my machine."

The free plan includes a monthly allowance of Codespace hours, plenty for learning and occasional use. Codespaces stop when idle, so you are not burning hours accidentally.

## Local vs. cloud: the practical split

**Work locally** for your daily projects: it is faster, works offline, and your AI coding tools run best there. **Reach for Codespaces** for quick experiments, unfamiliar repos, and machines that are not yours. **Host finished static work on Pages.** Together, they mean you can build, test, and publish from anywhere with a browser, while keeping your serious work on your own machine.

lessons.title: Repos Plus AI Coding Tools, and Your Portfolio Strategy
lessons.bodyMd:
## AI tools speak git

Modern AI coding assistants, Claude Code, Cursor, and their cousins, are designed to work inside git repositories. They read your project structure, understand your file history, and operate on branches like a human teammate. When you point one at a folder that is not a git repo, it still works, but you lose the safety net. When you point it at a repo, every AI-generated change becomes diffable, reviewable, and reversible.

Make this a rule: **no AI coding session starts outside a git repository.** Initialize one (`git init`) or clone one before the first prompt. The AI goes fast; git makes fast safe.

## The checkpoint habit

AI assistants can rewrite half your project in one response. That is powerful and terrifying. The defense is the checkpoint habit: commit before asking the AI to do anything significant.

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Checkpoint before AI refactor of auth module"
```

If the AI's output is brilliant, keep going. If it is a mess, restore from the last commit, and you have lost nothing but the prompt. Professionals working with AI commit far more often than they did before AI, precisely because the blast radius of each change is larger. Small checkpoints, constantly.

Review AI-generated diffs like you would a colleague's PR: `git diff` before every commit, read what actually changed, understand it before you snapshot it. "The AI wrote it" is never a substitute for understanding your own project.

## The secret rule: never commit secrets

AI tools need API keys, and beginners constantly commit them by accident. A `.env` file with your keys, pushed to a public repo, is visible to the entire internet within seconds, and bots scan GitHub for leaked keys continuously.

The defense is a `.gitignore` file listing what git must never track:

```
.env
*.pem
node_modules/
```

Create it before your first commit. If you use AI-generated code, ask the assistant to check for hardcoded secrets before committing. If a key ever does leak, do not just delete the file: **revoke and regenerate the key immediately**, because git history remembers everything. Deleting the file does not unpublish the secret.

## Your portfolio strategy

Your GitHub profile is your resume. Treat it like one:

**Pin 3 to 4 strong projects.** Each pinned repo needs: a clear README with what it does and how to run it, a screenshot or demo GIF, and a live link (Pages, Vercel, wherever it runs). A stranger should understand the project in thirty seconds.

**Build in public.** Commit regularly, write about what you learn, keep issues for your roadmap. The contribution graph fills naturally, and the history shows how you think.

**Quality over quantity.** Two projects you can explain deeply beat twenty tutorial clones. Interviewers will ask "walk me through this one." Make sure every pinned repo is one you would enjoy discussing.

**Connect it all.** Profile README introduces you, pinned repos prove it, Pages site presents it, LinkedIn and resume link to it. One coherent story, everywhere.

You started this guide not knowing what version control was. You are finishing it with a safety net for AI-speed building, a collaboration workflow professionals use daily, free hosting, automation, and a portfolio strategy. That is not beginner territory anymore. Ship something.
